description: A dreamy Lover-era outtake Taylor Swift recorded in 2019, shelved, then surprise-released in March 2023 after a leaked demo went viral — a thank-you note to every girlfriend who came before her.

pops.text: Vault track alert: Swift recorded this during sessions for her 2019 album Lover, then left it off the record.
She wrote and produced it with Louis Bell and Frank Dukes, the hitmakers behind much of Lover's glossy pop sound.
The concept flips the jealous-ex song: she thanks her partner's former girlfriends for shaping the man she loves.
A demo leaked online in February 2023 and went viral on TikTok, with fans campaigning for an official release.
Swift answered the fans: she surprise-released it on March 17, 2023, hours before the Eras Tour opened in Arizona.
It was one of four songs she dropped that night, alongside three Taylor's Version re-recordings from her vault-clearing era.
The release landed on The More Lover Chapter, a streaming EP gathering extra songs from the Lover world.
No radio push, no video — it still debuted at No. 12 on the Billboard Hot 100 on streams and sales alone.
That debut made it Swift's 189th career Hot 100 entry, extending her record for the most chart hits among women.
There is no official music video — this official audio upload is the song's home on YouTube.

title: All of the Girls You Loved Before
David Bowie
description: Phish's epic Junta instrumental whose entire lyric is two names — 'David Bowie' and 'UB40' — chanted over a twisting, tempo-shifting groove before the song opens into one of the band's darkest, most exploratory jams.

pops.text: Yes, that's the whole lyric: 'David Bowie' and 'UB40,' repeated. Relix flagged it back in October 1989 — an 11-minute, mostly instrumental epic built on a two-name chant.
It's from Junta, Phish's debut album, recorded at Euphoria Sound Studios in Revere, Massachusetts in 1988 and first sold as a self-produced cassette at gigs.
Despite the title, the song has nothing to do with the actual David Bowie — Trey Anastasio just liked the joke of chanting two wildly unrelated acts' names over a fiendishly complex groove.
Listen to how much is going on under the chant: tempo changes, a Latin-like lilt, Mike Gordon's slap bass and Page McConnell switching between lead and rhythm piano.
First played live in 1986, 'David Bowie' quickly became one of the band's go-to improvisation vehicles, in the same late-'80s class as 'Run Like an Antelope' and 'You Enjoy Myself.'
Phish.net counts it among a select group of just 10 Phish songs performed more than 400 times — rarefied air for a song with essentially no words.
In its 1993–95 peak, 'Bowie' was a super-heavyweight jam song, one of the few that could go as deep and dark as 'Tweezer' or 'Mike's Song' on any given night.
The jam's signature is tension: dissonant, mean, coiled playing that Phish fans cite — along with 'Antelope' — as the origin of the band's dark, exploratory style.
Live tradition: during the intro's hi-hat section, Trey loves weaving in teases of other songs — fans call it 'hi-hat hijinx.' A 1989 Syracuse version smuggles in three different tunes.
Birthday hijinks, 2/18/89: the band swapped the 'UB40' lyric to 'Fish's Birthday' for drummer Jon Fishman, then ordered him to do 100 pushups. The chant is flexible; the jam is forever.

description: A hopeful standout from R.E.M.'s Lifes Rich Pageant (1986), named for Ohio's Cuyahoga River — the river that famously caught fire — and sung like an invitation to start the country over.

pops.text: From Lifes Rich Pageant (1986), R.E.M.'s fourth album, and a fan-voted favorite deep cut ever since.
All four members — Berry, Buck, Mills and Stipe — share the songwriting credit, as they did throughout the band's career.
Producer Don Gehman, borrowed from John Mellencamp's team, gave the band a bigger, clearer sound than their earlier murk.
The album was recorded at Mellencamp's Belmont Mall studio in Indiana, far from the band's Athens, Georgia home base.
The title names the Cuyahoga River, which flows through Cleveland into Lake Erie.
'We burned the river down' is literal history: the polluted Cuyahoga famously caught fire several times, most notably in 1969.
The 1969 fire became a symbol of the pollution crisis and helped fuel the young environmental movement in America.
It opens with an invitation: 'Let's put our heads together and start a new country up' — protest sung as optimism.
The album's title, apostrophe deliberately missing, came from a line Peter Buck spotted in the 1964 film A Shot in the Dark.
Never a single and given no period video, Cuyahoga grew purely by word of mouth into one of R.E.M.'s most loved songs.

title: Cuyahoga

description: The gentlest moment on the Stones' psychedelic detour Their Satanic Majesties Request (1967) — harpsichord, strings and a singalong chorus, released as a US single that reached No. 25.

pops.text: From Their Satanic Majesties Request (1967), the Stones' full dive into psychedelia, recorded at Olympic Studios in London.
Written by Mick Jagger and Keith Richards, it started life under working titles like 'She Comes in Colours' and 'Lady Fair.'
That courtly piano and harpsichord is Nicky Hopkins, the session pianist who quietly starred on many Stones records.
The string arrangement is by a pre-fame John Paul Jones, two years before he co-founded Led Zeppelin.
Brian Jones colors the track with Mellotron, the era's magic keyboard, stocked with taped orchestral sounds.
In December 1967 it was released as a US single, paired with the cosmic rocker '2000 Light Years from Home.'
The single reached No. 25 on the Billboard Hot 100 — a hit built on harpsichord and strings, not blues riffs.
For decades the band almost never played it live; it returned in Chile in 2016 for the first time in 18 years.
This official lyric video, made by Yes Please Productions, arrived in 2017 for the album's 50th anniversary era.
Its kaleidoscope imagery made it a natural for TV ads and trailers, introducing the song to generations who missed 1967.

title: She's a Rainbow

description: A Michael Houser song from Widespread Panic's 1986 Athens club days that never landed on a studio album — it lived entirely on stage, including this official-channel performance from the first Bonnaroo.

pops.text: Vacation dates to 1986, developed while the young band played Monday nights at Athens, Georgia's Uptown Lounge.
It was written by founding guitarist Michael Houser, though the band shared all writing credits in the Houser era.
The band itself was named for Houser: 'Panic' was his nickname, earned from his once-frequent panic attacks.
Oddity: this beloved staple was never put on a studio album — the band's archive lists it among their unreleased originals.
Houser's signature sound came from a volume pedal, worked constantly to make his guitar swell and sing.
After the band's seated 1996 Sit 'n' Ski tour, Houser found playing sitting down so comfortable he sat for every show after.
This video is the official channel's upload from the first Bonnaroo festival, on June 22, 2002.
That Bonnaroo performance was the last Vacation Houser ever played — the band never performed it with him again.
Houser died of pancreatic cancer on August 10, 2002, at 40, weeks after that final festival run.
The song stayed in the repertoire as a tribute staple; in 2018 it opened a show for the first time ever, at Atlanta's Fox Theatre.

title: Vacation

description: Pigpen's swaggering blues shuffle, sung by Ron McKernan himself and preserved on Europe '72 (1972) — remarkably, the one track on that heavily polished live album with no studio overdubs at all.

pops.text: Sung by Ron 'Pigpen' McKernan, the Dead's original bluesman, who co-wrote it with lyricist Robert Hunter.
It debuted on July 31, 1971, in New Haven — the same show where another Hunter classic, Sugaree, was first played.
This official video captures the band at the Fox Theatre in St. Louis on December 10, 1971.
Pianist Keith Godchaux had joined the band only weeks earlier, beginning the Dead's great two-keyboard era.
The song was played just 50 times in total — a short, intense life in the repertoire.
Yet the band played it at every single show of the celebrated Europe '72 tour, all 22 of them.
The Europe '72 album version comes from the Lyceum Theatre in London, at the tour's very end.
Europe '72 was famously sweetened with overdubs — except this song. Mr. Charlie is the album's one untouched live track.
It was Pigpen's final original contribution to a Grateful Dead album; the song vanished from setlists when he died in 1973.
Decades later, Phil Lesh & Friends and Dead & Company revived it, returning Pigpen's shuffle to the stage.

title: Mr. Charlie
The Mountains Win Again
description: Blues Traveler's gentle acoustic ballad from Four (1994) — bassist Bobby Sheehan's lone composition on the band's breakthrough album, sung by John Popper with slide guitar from Warren Haynes. It became a 1995 single and a lasting fan favorite.

pops.text: Four, released September 13, 1994, paired the band's harmonica fireworks with its most tender song — this one.
Bassist Bobby Sheehan wrote it — his only composition on the entire album.
Guest slide guitar comes from Warren Haynes of the Allman Brothers Band and Gov't Mule.
John Popper sings it straight, letting the lyric's plainspoken heartbreak do the heavy lifting.
Its refrain lands on a stoic shrug — 'men are not to cry' — right before the tears come anyway.
Four was produced by Michael Barbiero and Steve Thompson.
Released as a single in 1995, after 'Run-Around' and 'Hook' had made the band stars.
It climbed to No. 14 on Billboard's Adult Alternative Airplay chart.
Its music video was directed by Ken Fox.
Decades on, it still turns up in Blues Traveler setlists, from Red Rocks to the Capitol Theatre.

title: A Day in the Life
description: The sprawling finale of Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band (1967): John Lennon's newspaper-inspired verses stitched to Paul McCartney's everyday morning rush by two tidal waves of orchestra, closing with the most famous final chord in rock.

pops.text: The closing track of Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band, released in the spring of 1967.
John Lennon built his verses from Daily Mail stories, including the fatal car crash of Guinness heir Tara Browne.
The potholes are real too: Lennon read about 4,000 holes in the roads of Blackburn, Lancashire.
Paul McCartney's bright middle section — oversleeping, catching a bus — began life as a separate, unfinished song.
Between the sections sat 24 empty bars; road manager Mal Evans counted them off while the band decided what belonged there.
The answer: a 40-piece orchestra, each player scored to slide from their instrument's lowest note to its highest.
The formally dressed orchestra musicians were handed party novelties to wear — false noses and gorilla-paw gloves among them.
The BBC initially banned the song over the line 'I'd love to turn you on.'
That final E-major chord: Lennon, McCartney, Starr and Mal Evans at three pianos, nine attempts to land it — and it rings for over 40 seconds.
After it fades, the original vinyl hid a 15-kilohertz whistle only dogs could hear, plus a loop of gibberish in the run-out groove.

title: Mahgeetah
description: My Morning Jacket's soaring opener to It Still Moves (2003) — a Jim James hymn to his guitar — captured here in the band's official Bonnaroo 2011 performance video, from a festival where 'Mahgeetah' has rattled stages for decades.

pops.text: It opens It Still Moves (2003), the band's third album and its major-label debut on ATO Records.
Frontman Jim James wrote every song on the album, this one included.
The title is James's own slurred word for his guitar — 'mah geetah' — which he sings to like a sweetheart.
This video comes from the band's set on Bonnaroo's What Stage on June 10, 2011.
Bonnaroo is sacred ground for this band — their legendary 2004 festival set there also opened with this very song.
The track was issued as one of the album's singles in 2003.
It even turned up in a beer commercial, carrying Jim James's falsetto to a lot of unsuspecting TV sets.
Setlist archives credit the song with more than 500 live performances.
In 2016, It Still Moves got a deluxe reissue — James remixed the album himself and unearthed an early 'Mahgeetah' demo.
It remains a signature moment: in 2022, Trey Anastasio joined the band in Mexico to tear through it as an encore.

artist: Nathan Lane, Ernie Sabella, Jason Weaver & Joseph Williams
description: Timon and Pumbaa's problem-free philosophy lesson from The Lion King (1994), written by Elton John and Tim Rice and sung by Nathan Lane, Ernie Sabella and the two singing voices of Simba.

pops.text: From The Lion King (1994): music by Elton John, lyrics by Tim Rice, the team behind the film's whole songbook.
'Hakuna matata' is a real Swahili phrase meaning 'no worries' — Rice picked it up while traveling in Kenya.
Nathan Lane voices meerkat Timon; Ernie Sabella is warthog Pumbaa — Broadway timing in cartoon form.
Young Simba's singing voice is Jason Weaver; the grown Simba who joins later is sung by Joseph Williams.
Williams had a day job in rock: he was a lead singer of Toto, of 'Africa' fame.
An earlier version of this slot in the film was 'The Warthog Rhapsody,' a whole song about eating bugs.
Pumbaa's tragic backstory verse ends with the immortal stage whisper: 'Hey, Pumbaa — not in front of the kids!'
During the bridge's montage, Simba grows from cub to adult — years pass inside one chorus.
The song was nominated for the Best Original Song Oscar, one of three Lion King songs nominated that year.
Reggae star Jimmy Cliff cut his own single version in 1995, taking Timon and Pumbaa's motto to the charts.

title: Hakuna Matata
King Without a Crown
description: Matisyahu's signature breakthrough: a reggae-rock plea blending Hasidic devotion with hip-hop rhythm and beatboxing. Written before he had a record deal, it exploded via the 2005 Live at Stubb's version and carried him onto the pop charts.

pops.text: Matisyahu — born Matthew Paul Miller — has called this the very first song he ever wrote, his 'firstborn child.'
He co-wrote it with bassist Josh Werner, before the unlikely blend of reggae, Hasidic devotion and beatboxing made him a star.
It first appeared on his 2004 debut, Shake Off the Dust... Arise, released by the tiny JDub Records label.
The version that broke through was live — recorded February 19, 2005, at Stubb's in Austin, Texas.
The lyrics look toward redemption: the cry of '2000 years of galut' — exile — runs through the song.
Live at Stubb's climbed to No. 1 on Billboard's reggae albums chart and was certified gold.
As a single in 2006, the song reached No. 28 on the Billboard Hot 100 — a Hasidic reggae anthem in the pop Top 40.
It climbed even higher on alternative radio, reaching No. 7 on the Alternative Airplay chart.
The official video was directed by Paul Brown, who later shot Matisyahu's 'One Day' as well.
In 2011 he returned to that same Austin stage to record Live at Stubb's, Vol. II — this song's old home turf.

description: Sly & The Family Stone's plea for everyday equality, released as a single in late 1968 and a No. 1 hit for four weeks in 1969 — two minutes of joy with a revolution folded inside.

pops.text: Released as a single in November 1968, then featured on the landmark album Stand! in 1969.
Written by Sylvester Stewart — Sly Stone — the band's singer, producer and resident visionary.
The band itself made the song's point: an integrated, mixed-gender lineup was still radical on American stages in 1968.
It became the group's first No. 1, spending four weeks atop the Billboard Hot 100 in early 1969.
The song turned 'different strokes for different folks' into an everyday catchphrase.
Larry Graham's bass work here helped pioneer the funk bottom end that the next decade was built on.
The lyric name-checks the butcher, the banker, the drummer — and insists every one of them is the same underneath.
Even the nonsense syllables carry the message: 'scooby dooby doo' is for everybody, too.
Arrested Development reworked it into their 1992 hit 'People Everyday,' carrying Sly's sermon to a new generation.
Joan Jett covered it in 1983, and a new animated video in 2021 introduced the song to yet another one.

title: Everyday People

description: Rush's signature song and the opening track of Moving Pictures (1981): a modern-day warrior's portrait built on a synthesizer growl Geddy Lee stumbled on while sound-checking.

pops.text: Track one on Moving Pictures (1981), recorded at Le Studio in Morin-Heights, Quebec — Rush's biggest-selling album.
Drummer Neil Peart wrote the lyrics with Pye Dubois of Max Webster, adapting Dubois's poem 'Louis the Lawyer.'
That famous synthesizer growl began as a sound Geddy Lee found while testing his Oberheim synth at a soundcheck.
Lee plays the synth part and the bass, sings lead, and covers the pedals — three jobs at once, as usual.
The title nods to Mark Twain's character, recast as a proud, free-thinking 'modern-day warrior.'
This official video was filmed at Le Studio during the album sessions — the band at work, not acting.
As a single it reached No. 44 on the Hot 100, No. 8 on rock radio, and No. 25 in the UK.
Peart's fills after 'catch the spit' are an air-drummer's final exam — precision as showmanship.
Moving Pictures made Canadian trio Rush arena headliners in America without sanding off any of their complexity.
Four decades on, Tom Sawyer remains the band's most recognized song and the standard opener of Rush tributes everywhere.

title: Tom Sawyer

description: The thunderous opener of Who's Next (1971), salvaged from Pete Townshend's abandoned Lifehouse opera — part hard rock, part early electronica, and forever misnamed 'Teenage Wasteland.'

pops.text: The opening track of Who's Next (1971), the album rescued from Pete Townshend's collapsed Lifehouse rock opera.
The title is a mash-up of two Townshend heroes: spiritual teacher Meher Baba and minimalist composer Terry Riley.
That hypnotic pulsing pattern is Townshend playing a Lowrey organ through its marimba-repeat setting — 1971 electronica.
Townshend fed his musical ideas about Meher Baba's teachings into the synthesizer experiments behind this track.
Roger Daltrey sings the verses; Townshend takes the middle — 'Don't cry, don't raise your eye.'
Session great Nicky Hopkins plays the rolling piano part, as he did across Who's Next.
The wild violin solo at the end is Dave Arbus, of East of Eden, sawing away over the fade.
It was never a UK single, yet became one of the band's defining songs purely through albums and radio.
Everyone calls it 'Teenage Wasteland' after its refrain — Townshend has spent 50 years correcting people.
It sits in the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame's list of 500 Songs That Shaped Rock and Roll; this lyric video arrived in 2020.

title: Baba O'Riley

description: The opening track of the Violent Femmes' 1983 debut — two minutes of whispered verses, shouted choruses and one unforgettable riff, written by a Milwaukee teenager and beloved ever since.

pops.text: Track one on Violent Femmes (1983), the Milwaukee trio's debut, recorded in July 1982 and released the following April.
Gordon Gano wrote much of the album while still in high school — this angst is authentically teenaged.
The band was famously discovered busking: the Pretenders' James Honeyman-Scott heard them on a Milwaukee street and got them that night's opening slot.
Brian Ritchie's acoustic bass guitar gives the band its strange folk-punk bottom end — no electric bass, no drum kit thunder.
Drummer Victor DeLorenzo mostly plays brushes on a single snare drum, a stripped kit he called the 'tranceaphone.'
The whispered verse exploding into the shouted chorus became the template for a decade of alternative rock dynamics.
It was never released as a commercial single in 1983 — college radio and word of mouth did all the work.
The debut album took eight years to reach platinum, a slow-burn cult classic that never really charted.
The 1997 film Grosse Pointe Blank put it front and center, sending a new generation back to the original.
A video made for the film's era has Gano, playing an assassin, hunting a puppet of Socks, the Clinton family's cat.

title: Blister in the Sun
